source/pnas-2024-civil-war-mortality-est.title: PNAS 2024 Civil War Mortality Estimates
source/pnas-2024-civil-war-mortality-est.summary: A national estimate of about 698,000 Civil War deaths from full-count census records, with a bounding interval of roughly 50,000 either way (647,439 to 748,561), set against the conventional count of 618,222 and the roughly 750,000 (751,562, bounds 632,115 to 871,009) that Hacker's 1 percent census sample gives when recomputed by the authors. Also the finding that about 13 percent of military-age native-born white men in the core Confederate states died against about 5 percent in the core Union states.

extra.title: Caveats
extra.html: Read in full on 2026-09-25 from the Europe PMC full-text XML of the open-access copy (PMC11621511); pnas.org returns HTTP 403 to automated requests and the PMC web page shows a CAPTCHA, neither of which was bypassed. This is a Brief Report. The earlier citation gave 25 September 2024, which is the acceptance date; Europe PMC gives first publication as 18 November 2024. The claim that the toll was 'much greater in the Confederate states' concerns rates: about 13 percent of military-age native-born white men in the core Confederate states against about 5 percent in the core Union states. In absolute numbers the Union lost more men, about 400,000 or more against roughly 300,000 for the Confederacy on the paper's own tally. The estimate measures excess mortality, which includes deaths of veterans after the war and some civilian deaths, and it rests on standard assumptions for foreign-born and Black soldier deaths, which the census method cannot estimate.

source.citation: Barceló, J., Jensen, J. L., Peisakhin, L., and Zhai, H. 2024. 'New estimates of US Civil War mortality from full-census records.' Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 121(48): e2414919121. First published 18 November 2024.

source/pigati-et-al-2023-white-sands-foo.title: Pigati et al. 2023 White Sands Footprints

extra.title: Caveats
extra.html: Only the abstract was read (the PubMed record, fetched on 2026-09-25 through NCBI E-utilities). science.org returns HTTP 403 and the PubMed web page shows a cookie wall, neither of which was bypassed, and no open-access copy of the full paper turned up. This source therefore confirms only what the abstract says: the abstract calls the dated material 'terrestrial pollen' and the luminescence dating 'of sediments', so the wording 'conifer pollen', 'quartz' and the year of the first seed dates (2021), which the Peopling of the Americas note used to carry, is not confirmed here and was removed from that note until the full paper is read; sample counts, error ranges and methods are also unread. The abstract says the earlier seed ages were controversial because of possible old-carbon reservoir effects. Whether the age is universally accepted is not something the abstract can show; the vault treats it as well supported but contested, following Wikipedia on the Settlement of the Americas.

source/science-2021-amazonian-reforestat.title: Science 2021 Amazonian Reforestation Pollen Study
source/science-2021-amazonian-reforestat.summary: The finding, from 39 Amazonian fossil pollen records, that there was no synchronous reforestation event after European arrival and that at most sites land abandonment and forest regrowth began about 300 to 600 years before European arrival. The abstract frames this as a test of the hypothesis that a post-contact population collapse (an estimated 90 to 95 percent of Indigenous people in Amazonia) lowered atmospheric carbon dioxide around 1610 CE through reforestation, and it names pre-European pandemics, social strife and environmental change as possible causes of the earlier abandonments.

extra.title: Caveats
extra.html: Only the abstract was read (the PubMed record, fetched on 2026-09-25), together with the accepted-version supplementary materials in the University of Reading repository (methods and site tables, about 7,800 characters), which confirm that 39 lake-sediment records were used. science.org returns HTTP 403 and no open-access copy of the main paper was found, so its results and discussion were not read. The reply from Alexander Koch and colleagues, and the statement that Bush and McMichael think populations peaked and declined well before 1492, both appear in the Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands note but are not in the text read here; they came from press coverage seen only as search-result summaries and remain unverified. The paper challenges one hypothesis (post-1492 regrowth cooling the climate); it does not show that no post-contact depopulation occurred, and its abstract cites an estimated 90 to 95 percent loss of Indigenous people.

source.citation: Bush, M. B., Nascimento, M. N., Åkesson, C. M., Cárdenes-Sandí, G. M., Maezumi, S. Y., Behling, H., Correa-Metrio, A., Church, W., Huisman, S. N., Kelly, T., Mayle, F. E., and McMichael, C. N. H. 2021. 'Widespread reforestation before European influence on Amazonia.' Science 372(6541): 484-487.

extra.title: Caveats
extra.html: Only the abstract was read (the PubMed record, fetched on 2026-09-26). The full text was not reachable by any route that works for automated requests: routes tried without success were europepmc-fulltext, openalex-oa-pdf, publisher-direct, wayback (nph.onlinelibrary.wiley.com, onlinelibrary.wiley.com, web.archive.org answered HTTP 403 to automated requests), and no CAPTCHA, cookie wall or paywall was bypassed. This source therefore confirms only what the abstract states. The abstract confirms that maize (Zea mays subsp. mays) was transformed from the teosinte Z. mays subsp. parviglumis, that five major morphological differences separate them and that regions throughout the genome contributed. It gives no domestication date, no site or microfossil age and no figure for highland teosinte ancestry, so those details in the Domestication of Maize note were removed. An earlier caveat said they had been confirmed only in search summaries of related sources. An abstract-only source never moves a note toward reviewed.

extra.title: Caveats

source/wikipedia-on-tomb-of-cyrus.title: Wikipedia on Tomb of Cyrus
source/wikipedia-on-tomb-of-cyrus.summary: Supports Alexander's visit to the pillaged tomb and, per Arrian, his order to restore it, and the structure of a six-step platform with a gabled chamber.

source/wikipedia-on-tomyris.title: Wikipedia on Tomyris
source/wikipedia-on-tomyris.summary: Supports Tomyris as a 6th-century BC Massagetae queen known only from Herodotus, the 530 BC date of Cyrus's death in her battle, the marriage refusal, and the death of her son Spargapises.

extra.title: Caveats
extra.html: A general-audience encyclopedia article that retells Herodotus, so it verifies what the tradition says rather than what historically happened, and my read was a WebFetch extract of the page rather than a full-page reading.

extra.title: Caveats

extra.title: Caveats
